 About 

 The screening will be followed by a discussion with the film's director, Dr Imad Karam. The documentary tells the story of Jo Berry, whose father was killed in the 1984 Brighton bombing, and Pat Magee, the IRA volunteer responsible for planting the bomb. Years later, after a loss that could never be undone, the two chose to meet. What followed was not a search for closure, nor a straightforward story of forgiveness, but a relationship shaped by difficult conversations, persistent disagreement, curiosity, and a willingness to confront the human consequences of political violence. Following the screening, Dr Imad Karam, an award-winning British-Palestinian filmmaker, will discuss the making of the film and the questions that continue to shape it.

events.title: “It’s lucky that we live in Iceland”: Nordic exceptionalism and narratives of climate in/vulnerability in contemporary Iceland
events.venue: Scott Polar Research Institute, Lecture Theatre
events.speaker: Utsa Mukherjee (Education, Brunel University of London)
events.series: Scott Polar Research Institute - HCEP (Histories, Cultures, Environments and Politics) Research Seminars
events.description: While climate vulnerability, that is the geographical distribution of risks on account of the climate crisis, is widely discussed; relatively little scholarly attention has been paid to how colonial fantasies of climate invulnerability underpin climate inaction and justify the maintenance of status quo (Weatherill, 2025). This paper contributes to the emergent body of critical scholarship on the politics of climate in/vulnerability through a focus on contemporary Iceland. Drawing on in-depth interviews with more than 80 participants from across Iceland, who recognise the reality of anthropogenic climate change and are committed to climate action, we show how Iceland’s geographical location is invoked by participants to advance ideas of relative climate in/vulnerability of the island. Analysed through prisms of critical feminist and decolonial politics, these narratives assume two main forms. One portrays Iceland as geographically ‘lucky’, thereby less vulnerable to climate risks which are displaced onto far-off places ‘at risk’. The other sees Iceland as not doing enough to combat climate change, thereby exposing itself to future risks from ‘elsewhere’. We argue that these narratives of climate invulnerability are produced at the intersection of colonial imaginaries of geographical risks and widespread acceptance of Icelandic exceptionalism that obviates critical examination of current status quo. events.title: Kropotkin’s Anarchist Animals
events.venue: Small Lecture Theatre, Department of Geography
events.speaker: David Nally, University of Cambridge
events.series: Political Ecology Group Seminar Series
events.description: Anarchists have long argued that cooperation, more than competition, drives evolution. In that spirit, this seminar practises mutual aid of the most intimate kind, drawing generously on, and rarely straying beyond, the author’s own recent work (Nally 2026). Pyotr Kropotkin (1842–1921), perhaps the best-known anarchist of all, was a Russian geographer of royal lineage (he descended from the Rurik dynasty) who renounced the title of ‘Prince’ and devoted himself to the struggle against domination. He idolised Alexander von Humboldt, yet he declined the offer of a Chair in Geography at Cambridge because it required him to give up his pollical convictions. Natural scientists know Kropotkin for his pioneering analysis of ‘mutual aid’ among nonhumans, whereas social scientists know him better for his rigorous defence of anarchism as philosophy and ideal. While most scholars have held these two strands apart, this seminar argues that his studies of animal sociality were foundational to his political vision. For Kropotkin, humans and nonhumans co-evolved, sharing an entangled history and a repertoire of socially learned behaviours. Recognising this common origin – and, more broadly, the unity of all living matter – allowed Kropotkin to pose the most vital of political questions: what right does anyone have to rule over others? The seminar traces how Kropotkin’s animal studies led him to this thunderbolt of a thought, and asks what it demands of us today, in an age of resurgent authori

events.title: Can Courts Save the Environment Without Weakening Democracy? Rethinking Environmental Judicial Activism in South Asia
events.venue: The Umney Theatre, Robinson College, Grange Road, CB3 9AN
events.series: What's On at Robinson College
events.description:
In his lecture, Dr Jashim Chowdhury looks into the matter of the e nvironmental constitutionalism which has empowered courts to respond where political institutions appear unwilling or unable to act. In India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, however, this expansion of judicial authority raises a neglected question: can environmentally progressive judgments nevertheless be democratically deficient? 

 Drawing on his forthcoming book, Dr Chowdhury examines a pattern of environmental adjudication that is normatively ambitious but frequently less inclusive, less democratic and more combative than its objectives require. In his lecture he argues that the central challenge is not choosing between judicial activism and restraint, but reimagining the relationship between courts, legislatures, governments and affected communities. Bringing South Asian jurisprudence into conversation with deliberative democracy and dialogic judicial review, the lecture develops a model of collaborative environmental adjudication. Under this model, courts do not abandon rights enforcement; rather, they employ participatory and dialogue-promoting remedies that distribute responsibility, improve public justification and make environmental reform more democratically legitimate and institutionally sustainable.

 About What might it mean to live a flourishing life? And what is the relationship between flourishing and the virtues, especially justice? In this talk based on her recent book, Professor Angie Hobbs explores how Plato can help us with these urgent questions, and how he addresses the key issue of character formation, and why it never benefits us to return wrong for wrong. She shows how she has used his methodology, ideas and arguments in a variety of sectors to address contemporary issues in education, faith–secular debate, health care and the civil service, and invites the audience to discuss with her what further lessons can be applied. We are living in fast-moving and uncertain times and need ancient wisdom more than ever. Plato really does matter, right now! 
 Why Plato Matters Now (Bloomsbury 2025). angiehobbs.com 
 Angie Hobbs is Professor of the Public Understanding of Philosophy Emerita at the University of Sheffield. She gained a degree in Classics (First Class) and a PhD in Ancient Philosophy at the University of Cambridge.  About 

 Professor Elizabeth Shakman Hurd, Heaven Has A Wall.  
 Join us in  S2, Alison Richards Building  on Monday 30th November 2026   @ 5PM  for a discussion with Prof. Elizabeth Shakman Hurd on her book Heaven Has a Wall: Religion, Borders, and the Global United States , (University of Chicago Press, 2025)
 Abstract:  Everyone has a border story, but for American borders there is more going on than meets the eye. At times, the US ferociously enforces its borders, while at other times it circumvents or ignores them. events.venue: Institute of Criminology, Sidgwick Site, Cambridge CB3 9DA and online

events.series: Institute of Criminology
events.description:
This event is part of the Institute of Criminology's Public Guest Seminar Series for Michaelmas Term 2026. A drinks reception follows the talk. These events are free and everyone is welcome. Please register to attend either in-person or online by clicking the link at the bottom of this page. 
 About In Memoriam Andreas von Hirsch (1934-2026) 
 The Institute of Criminology is indebted to Andreas von Hirsch in many and profound ways. We will mention just three. First, because he was a valued member of the Institute for many years; second because he was an extraordinarily generous benefactor; and third because he was a towering intellectual figure in his own right. He was a pioneering force in taking seriously the connections between criminology and related fields – and both criminology and those other fields are much enriched by the interdisciplinary relationships his work contributed so decisively to emphasise. His work at the helm of the Committee for the Study of Incarceration (1976) continues to reward rereading – so much so that another workshop devoted to Doing Justice (the final “Report” of that Committee) is planned for 3-4 December (and had been planned before news of his passing reached its organizers). “Justice matters”, von Hirsch emphasised throughout his career: and it is a matter of justice – but also of immense gratitude – that we honour him with this memorial.

events.title: Counterfeit Procedure: How 'Digital Arrest' Fraud Simulates the State
events.venue: Webinar & Lecture Theatre 2, Computer Laboratory, William Gates Building
events.speaker: Shakti Avasthy, Indian Police Service
events.series: Computer Laboratory Security Seminar
events.description:
In the fraud known in India as 'digital arrest', victims are told by people posing as officers of several state agencies that they are under investigation, shown forged orders of the country's highest court, held under continuous video 'custody' for days, and instructed to move their savings into a 'supervised' account for verification. Recorded complaints rose from about 40,000 in 2022 to over 120,000 in 2024. This talk argues that the offence is not impersonation but institutional simulation: what the operators reproduce is not a person but the procedural form by which a state proceeds against a citizen - inter-agency referral, documentary authority, staged adjudication, custody - closely enough that compliance follows from recognising the procedure rather than believing any individual. Victims who verify are captured by the act of verifying. Drawing on one case reconstructed from the investigative record of a police commissionerate in India's National Capital Region, and six comparator cases from the public record, the talk sets out the architecture, the inversion of the burden of proof that makes it durable, and why the single most effective state intervention observed was not an arrest campaign but a public statement of a procedure the state never uses. It closes on the uncomfortable corollary: because the fraud borrows real authority rather than inventing it, its power rises with the capability of the state it imitates.

events.title: CFL/Cambridge Socio-Legal Group Seminar: 'The evolution of parenthood in Brazil: from the single-parent stigma to multiple parenthood'
events.venue: Faculty of Law, David Williams Building
events.description:
Date/time: 

 Monday 25 January 2027 

 1:00pm to 2:00pm

 Location: 

 Faculty of Law, David Williams Building

 G24

 About 

 Speaker: Professor João Costa-Neto (University of Brasília)
 Abstract: Brazilian family law has undergone a remarkable transformation: from a system built around marriage, biological descent and exclusive parenthood to one increasingly willing to recognise families as they are actually lived. This talk will trace that evolution, focusing on the rise of socioaffective parenthood and the idea that being a parent may result not only from biology, but also from care, responsibility and the social reality of family life. It then explores the most striking consequence of that shift: multiple parenthood, under which biological and socioaffective parents may coexist with equal legal status. Drawing on constitutional change, legal scholarship and recent case law, we will understand how Brazil moved from debating who the “real” parent is to accepting that, in some families, there may be more than one.
 This event is a hybrid event. If you are in Cambridge, please do join us in the Faculty. To attend online you must register via Zoom .

events.speaker: Professor Andrés Rodríguez-Pose, London School of Economics
events.series: St Catharine's Political Economy Seminar Series
events.description:
Speaker: Professor Andrés Rodríguez-Pose
 Talk Title: The two geographies of artificial intelligence: AI invention, AI use and regional economic performance in Europe
 Time: 18:00 -19:30 
 Location: Ramsden room, St Catharine's College 
 The seminar series is supported by the Cambridge Political Economy Society and the Economics and Policy Group at the Cambridge Judge Business School. 

 Talk Overview: :
 Artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to raise economic performance. Much less is known about where in Europe its economic returns land. This article distinguishes between AI invention —the creation of new AI technologies— and AI use —their deployment in production— and asks which of the two is associated with regional economic performance. AI invention is measured through AI patent applications and AI use through AI labor demand, the number of AI-skill mentions per 1,000 online job advertisements, drawn from Cedefop’s Skills-OVATE data and validated against firm-level adoption. Because hiring and growth are jointly determined, regional AI labor demand is instrumented with a shift-share prediction based on pre-period industrial structure and national trends in AI hiring by sector. Estimates for 191 European NUTS-2 regions over 2022–2024 reveal a clear asymmetry. Regions with higher AI labor demand grew faster in GDP per capita and labor productivity, with no detectable change in employment. AI patenting shows no association with growth.
